questiontext.text: In Michael Feathers' sense, a seam is:

answer.text: A place where you can change a program's behaviour without editing the code in that place

feedback.text: Correct — a seam lets you substitute behaviour (e.g. swap a dependency) without modifying the code at that point.

answer.text: A defect deliberately injected into the code to test the test suite

feedback.text: That is a seeded fault/mutant, not a seam.

answer.text: A line of code that always contains a bug

feedback.text: A seam is a point of substitutable behaviour, not a guaranteed bug.

answer.text: A boundary between two microservices on the network

feedback.text: A seam is a code-level place to alter behaviour, not a network boundary.

generalfeedback.text: Feathers defines a seam as a place where you can alter a program's behaviour without editing in that place. Injecting a dependency creates such a seam: a test can substitute a double there without touching the function's body.

questiontext.text: Dependency injection (DI) means:

answer.text: Passing a dependency in from outside (e.g. as a parameter) instead of creating or reading it inside the function

feedback.text: Correct — the collaborator is supplied to the code rather than constructed or fetched inside it.

answer.text: Injecting a fault into a running program to see how it copes

feedback.text: That is fault injection, not dependency injection.

answer.text: Copying a global variable into every function that needs it

feedback.text: Reaching for a global is exactly what DI replaces; DI passes the dependency in explicitly.

answer.text: Automatically generating test cases from the code

feedback.text: That is test generation, unrelated to how a dependency is supplied.

generalfeedback.text: Dependency injection supplies a function's collaborators from outside — typically as parameters — instead of having the function build them with new or read them from a global. This creates a seam where a test can substitute a double.

questiontext.text: A test double is:

answer.text: A stand-in object substituted for a real dependency during a test

feedback.text: Correct — stubs, mocks and fakes are all test doubles that replace a real collaborator under test.

answer.text: A second copy of the test that runs in parallel

feedback.text: That is not a double; a double replaces a dependency, not the test itself.

answer.text: The production implementation of a dependency

feedback.text: A double stands in for the real implementation; it is not the real thing.

answer.text: A tool that measures code coverage

feedback.text: That is a coverage tool, not a test double.

generalfeedback.text: A test double is any object put in place of a real dependency so the code under test can be exercised in isolation — stub, mock, fake, dummy and spy are the common kinds. Each testability seam is a place where a double can be dropped in.

name.text: Why a global singleton read hurts testability

questiontext.text: In charge(), the line const cfg = Config.instance(); reads a global singleton. Why does this hurt testability?

answer.text: It is a hidden input the test cannot set or substitute, because it is fetched inside the function

feedback.text: Correct — a test has no seam to supply a different config; the dependency is pinned inside the code.

answer.text: Singletons run slower than injected objects

feedback.text: The problem is control, not speed.

answer.text: Global reads always throw an exception under test

feedback.text: They do not throw; the issue is that the test cannot substitute the value.

answer.text: It makes the function return the wrong type

feedback.text: It does not change the return type; it removes the test's control over config.

generalfeedback.text: Reading a global singleton pulls a hidden input straight into the function. Because the test never passes it in, there is no seam to substitute a test config — reducing controllability. The fix is to inject a config parameter.

name.text: Why a hard-coded new hurts testability

questiontext.text: In charge(), the line const gw = new PaymentGateway(); constructs its collaborator directly. Why does this hurt testability?

answer.text: The dependency is created inside the function, so a test cannot swap it for a double

feedback.text: Correct — hard-coding new pins the real gateway; there is no seam to substitute one.

answer.text: Using new is a syntax error in test code

feedback.text: new is valid; the problem is that the collaborator cannot be substituted.

answer.text: Constructors cannot be called more than once

feedback.text: They can; the issue is the test cannot replace the constructed object.

answer.text: It doubles the memory the function uses

feedback.text: The concern is substitutability, not memory.

generalfeedback.text: Constructing the gateway with new inside charge() binds the code to the real implementation. A test cannot reach in to replace it, so the real gateway (network, side effects) runs. Injecting the collaborator opens a seam for a double.

name.text: Why the real clock hurts testability

questiontext.text: In charge(), the line const at = Date.now(); reads the real wall clock. Why does this hurt testability?

answer.text: The time changes on every run, so a test cannot pin it to assert on a fixed timestamp

feedback.text: Correct — the real clock is a nondeterministic input the test cannot control.

answer.text: Date.now() returns a string that is hard to parse

feedback.text: It returns a number; the real issue is that the value is uncontrollable.

answer.text: Reading the clock deletes the previous timestamp

feedback.text: It does not; the problem is nondeterminism, not data loss.

answer.text: The clock is only available in production builds

feedback.text: It is available under test too; but its value cannot be pinned without a seam.

generalfeedback.text: The wall clock is a nondeterministic source: Date.now() differs on every run, so a test can never assert on an exact timestamp. Injecting a clock lets a test substitute a fake that returns a fixed time.

questiontext.text: In charge(), the line const id = Math.random().toString(36); uses the real RNG. Why does this hurt testability?

answer.text: The value differs on every run, so a test cannot make the generated id deterministic

feedback.text: Correct — real randomness is a nondeterministic input the test cannot control.

answer.text: Math.random() is too slow to call inside a test

feedback.text: Speed is not the issue; determinism is.

answer.text: Random numbers are always negative

feedback.text: Math.random() returns a value in [0,1); the problem is it is not controllable.

answer.text: Calling it changes the config singleton

feedback.text: It does not touch config; it just produces an uncontrollable value.

generalfeedback.text: The RNG is a nondeterministic source: Math.random() yields a different id each run, so a test cannot assert on the id. Injecting a seeded rng lets a test substitute a deterministic generator.

answer.text: Inject a seeded rng (pass a generator in, e.g. deps.rng.id())

feedback.text: Scaling a random value is still random and uncontrollable.

feedback.text: Averaging real randomness is still nondeterministic.

answer.text: Convert the number to a string with a fixed prefix

feedback.text: The random part remains uncontrollable; no seam is created.

generalfeedback.text: The fix is to inject a seeded rng (deps.rng.id()) instead of calling Math.random(), opening a seam where a test substitutes a deterministic generator.

answer.text: Removing the pinned dependencies so each one becomes substitutable by a test

feedback.text: Frequency of runs is unrelated to designing the code for substitutability.

name.text: Score and capabilities for newdep plus random

questiontext.text: A learner applies only the newdep and random fixes. What score and which unlocked capabilities result?

answer.text: 50% (2/4); force the gateway to fail, and make the generated id deterministic

feedback.text: Correct — two fixes give 2/4, unlocking the gateway and rng capabilities.

answer.text: 50% (2/4); assert on a fixed timestamp, and supply a test config

feedback.text: Those are the clock and config capabilities, which were not applied here.

answer.text: 75% (3/4); force the gateway to fail, and make the generated id deterministic

feedback.text: Only two fixes are applied, so the score is 2/4, not 3/4.

answer.text: 25% (1/4); force the gateway to fail

feedback.text: Two distinct fixes are applied, so the score is 2/4 and two capabilities are unlocked.

generalfeedback.text: Two applied fixes give 2/4 = 50%. The newdep fix unlocks "force the gateway to fail" and the random fix unlocks "make the generated id deterministic".

questiontext.text: Why does making every dependency substitutable make charge() testable?

answer.text: Once each dependency can be substituted, a test can control all inputs and observe all effects, which is what testability requires

feedback.text: Correct — substitutable dependencies give the test both controllability and observability.

answer.text: Because substitutable code always runs faster

feedback.text: Speed is not the point; control and observation are.

answer.text: Because injected dependencies never contain bugs

feedback.text: They can still have bugs; injection just makes the unit controllable in a test.

answer.text: Because the function then needs no dependencies at all

feedback.text: It still has dependencies; they are simply supplied by the test.

generalfeedback.text: Testability is controllability plus observability. When every dependency is substitutable, a test can drive all inputs (config, gateway behaviour, time, id) and observe the effects — so substitutability is precisely what makes the unit testable.

name.text: Fix that only removes a hidden input

questiontext.text: Which single fix removes a hidden input but does not remove nondeterminism and does not enable forcing a failure?

answer.text: Inject the config parameter (the global fix)

feedback.text: Correct — it removes the hidden global input; it is not a nondeterministic source, and forcing a failure is the gateway's capability.

answer.text: Inject a clock (the clock fix)

feedback.text: The clock fix removes nondeterminism, so it does not fit.

answer.text: Inject a seeded rng (the random fix)

feedback.text: The rng fix removes nondeterminism, so it does not fit.

answer.text: Inject the gateway (the newdep fix)

feedback.text: The gateway fix is exactly the one that enables forcing a failure, so it does not fit.

generalfeedback.text: The global-config fix removes a hidden input (improving controllability). It is not one of the nondeterminism sources (clock, rng), and forcing a failure is unlocked by the gateway fix — so the config fix uniquely matches.

name.text: Fixes for a fixed time and deterministic id

questiontext.text: A test must assert on both a fixed timestamp and a deterministic id. Which fixes are needed, and what score results?

answer.text: Inject the clock and inject the seeded rng; score 50% (2/4)

feedback.text: Correct — the clock pins the time, the rng pins the id; two of four dependencies are substitutable.

answer.text: Inject the config and inject the gateway; score 50% (2/4)

feedback.text: Those unlock config and failure-forcing, not a fixed time or deterministic id.

answer.text: Inject the clock only; score 25% (1/4)

feedback.text: The clock pins the time but not the id; the rng is also needed.

answer.text: Inject all four; score 100% (4/4)

feedback.text: Only the clock and rng are required for these two assertions; that is 2/4.

generalfeedback.text: A fixed timestamp needs the clock fix; a deterministic id needs the rng fix. Applying exactly those two gives 2/4 = 50%.

questiontext.text: Applying the clock fix then the global fix yields the same score as applying the global fix then the clock fix.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — testabilityOf counts the set of applied fixes, so order does not matter: either way it is 2/4.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: The score depends only on which fixes are applied, not the order; both orders give 2/4.

generalfeedback.text: Score = applied/4, computed from the set of applied fixes (deduped, in fixture order). The order in which the learner toggles them does not change the result: two distinct fixes give 2/4 = 50% either way.

name.text: Mock versus stub for the gateway

questiontext.text: A test wants to verify that charge() calls the gateway with the right arguments, not merely receive a canned return value. Which double, enabled by which fix, does this need?

answer.text: A mock, enabled by injecting the gateway collaborator

feedback.text: Correct — a mock verifies interactions; a stub would only return canned values.

answer.text: A stub, enabled by injecting the gateway collaborator

feedback.text: A stub returns canned values but does not verify the call; the gateway seam here maps to a mock.

answer.text: A fake, enabled by injecting a clock

feedback.text: A fake clock pins time; it does not verify a gateway call.

answer.text: A stub, enabled by injecting a seeded rng

feedback.text: The rng stub fixes the id; it says nothing about the gateway call.

generalfeedback.text: Verifying the interaction (right method, right arguments) is behaviour verification, the job of a mock. In this fixture the gateway seam maps to a mock, so injecting the gateway is the enabling fix.

questiontext.text: All four fixes are object seams, yet they enable three different doubles (stub, mock, fake). What does this show?

answer.text: The seam type (where you substitute) is independent of the double (what you substitute); one seam kind can host different doubles depending on the test's goal

feedback.text: Correct — object seams provide the substitution point; the choice of stub, mock or fake depends on what the test needs.

answer.text: Each seam type can enable only one kind of double

feedback.text: The opposite: one seam type (object) here hosts stubs, a mock, and a fake.

answer.text: Object seams can only ever enable stubs

feedback.text: Here object seams also enable a mock and a fake.

answer.text: The double determines the seam type

feedback.text: They are independent; the same object seam hosts different doubles.

generalfeedback.text: Seam type and double type are orthogonal. All four fixes use the same object seam, but the test picks the double — stub for canned config/id, mock to verify the gateway call, fake for a working fixed clock — according to its goal.
